definition: Merriam-Webster's Word of the Day for November 28, 2026 is: parse &#149; \PARSS\&nbsp; &#149; verb To parse or parse through something is to study it by looking closely at its parts, or in other words to analyze it critically. In grammar and linguistics, parse means "to divide (a sentence) into grammatical parts and identify the parts and their relations to each other." // The lawyer meticulously parsed the wording of the final contract to be sure that her client would get all that he was asking for. See the entry > Examples: "The stakes will be high for the summit, and every word out of each leader's mouth will be parsed ." — Kevin Breuninger, CNBC , 12 May 2026
did_you_know: ? If parse brings up memories of learning about nouns, verbs, and other parts of speech in school, you've done your homework regarding this word. Parsing sentences, after all, is part and parcel of learning to read and write. Parse comes from the first element of the Latin term for "part of speech," pars orationis . It's an old word that has been used since at least the mid-1500s, but it took another couple centuries for parse to graduate to its extended, non-grammar-related sense of "to examine in a minute way" or "to analyze critically." Remember this extended sense, and you'll really be at the head of the class.
